title: Silence and Undertow
premise: Mirabel Okafor, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost her sense of taste after her sister's drowning twenty years ago, returns to her estranged family for her mother's funeral. A stranger at the service calls the family by their old neighborhood name—a name they buried along with the truth of what happened the night Ada died—and Mirabel realizes her entire family's silence was arranged, not natural. As the last bus route to the old neighborhood is about to be rerouted, erasing the place itself, she investigates what really happened, discovering that her father covered up a neighbor's crime to protect the family's survival and that Ada's death was witnessed by a child who has been waiting decades to speak. In the end, Mirabel chooses testimony over protection: she publishes the truth under her own byline, sacrificing her career and her family's fragile peace, but recovering—literally and figuratively—her ability to taste.
about_author: M. M. Galloway is the pen name of a former food writer who spent a decade covering restaurant culture before turning to fiction about the things families refuse to say at the table. They live near a coastal city whose oldest bus line was recently decommissioned, an event that inspired this novel.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. At a high-profile tasting menu, she writes glowing prose for food she cannot taste, then learns of her mother's death mid-review. The chapter establishes her polished detachment and the private grief beneath it. Emotional beat: numb competence cracking at its first seam.

chapters.title: Return Without Luggage
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She arrives at the family home where her brother Chidi and aunt have already begun arranging the funeral like a performance. Everyone performs grief correctly; no one mentions Ada. Emotional beat: the uncanny choreography of a family rehearsing silence.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. At the wake, an elderly stranger greets the family as 'the Nwosu-Okafor household from Ferrier Street'—a name and address expunged from all family memory. Her father's old friend ushers the man out too quickly. Emotional beat: a single word splitting open twenty years.

chapters.title: What We Served the Mourners
chapters.summary: Chidi's POV. He manages the funeral catering with controlling precision, revealing through his obsession with feeding people how the family substitutes provision for honesty. He warns Mirabel, gently, not to 'go digging.' Emotional beat: love expressed as enforced quiet.

chapters.title: Ferrier Street, Last Stop
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She rides the doomed bus route to the old neighborhood, now half-demolished, and finds the house where Ada drowned in the flooded quarry behind it. A woman watching from a porch recognizes her instantly. Emotional beat: memory returning as physical vertigo.

chapters.title: The Porch Witness
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The porch woman, Grace, claims only to have known Ada 'a little,' but her phrasing mirrors details Mirabel never told anyone. Grace gives her a phone number written on a funeral card—her mother's. Emotional beat: suspicion braided with longing.

chapters.title: Taste Memory
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Mirabel's POV. The last meal she truly tasted: jollof rice in the old kitchen the night before Ada died. The chapter renders the family before the silence, full of noise and argument and appetite. Emotional beat: devastating warmth by contrast.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Going through her mother's papers, she finds a legal settlement document: hush money paid by the Okafor family to another family—or received from them? The signature dates are three days after Ada's drowning. Emotional beat: the discovery that silence had paperwork.

chapters.title: Brother, Keeper
chapters.summary: Chidi's POV. Confronted, Chidi admits he knew there was a payment but was told as a teenager it was 'compensation for damages'—and he chose not to ask more because asking would have broken the family. Emotional beat: complicity as an act of devotion.

chapters.title: Grace, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Grace finally talks: her son Emeka was at the quarry that night. He saw something. He was eleven years old, and he has not spoken a full sentence since—not from trauma alone, but because someone made him understand what saying it would cost both families. Emotional beat: horror arriving quietly, in a kitchen over tea.

chapters.title: The Man at the Funeral
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She tracks down the stranger, Mr. Anozie, her father's former business partner. He confirms the arrangement: Mirabel's father paid to keep Emeka's account of the night out of any inquiry, believing—or claiming—he was protecting everyone. Emotional beat: the sickening realization that her beloved father built the wall.

chapters.title: What Emeka Saw
chapters.summary: Emeka's POV, fragmented and halting. Now in his thirties, he pieces together the night in broken syntax: two older boys, a dare, Ada slipping, and one boy running for help while the other stood watching—and that second boy was not a stranger. Emotional beat: testimony surfacing like a body rising in water.

chapters.title: The Second Boy
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The description matches her cousin Daniel—the cousin who became a judge. The man who now sentences others within the law was present at the lawless center of the family's founding wound. Emotional beat: vertigo of realizing justice and crime share a bloodline.

chapters.title: Dinner Invitation
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. Daniel hosts Mirabel for dinner, serving dishes chosen to unsettle her, probing how much she knows. He is brilliant, charming, and utterly certain that the past should stay buried for everyone's good—including hers. Emotional beat: menace wearing the mask of hospitality.

chapters.title: Rerouted
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The bus route is officially decommissioned; the quarry site is fenced for development. Time is literally closing over the evidence. Grace tells her Emeka will testify—but only if Mirabel stands beside him publicly, sharing the risk. Emotional beat: the cost of truth becoming concrete and personal.

chapters.title: Father's Ledger
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Among her mother's effects she finds her father's private ledger: years of payments to Grace's family, annotated in his hand—not 'hush money' but 'debt, unpaid.' He knew Emeka's silence was purchased with a life. Emotional beat: grief for a father refigured as accountability.

chapters.title: The Family Vote
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, rotating short sections. Mirabel convenes the surviving family and lays everything on the table. Chidi wavers, the aunt pleads for unity, Daniel threatens litigation, and old Mirabel would have smiled and ended the conversation. Instead she waits. Emotional beat: the family's architecture of silence collapsing in real time.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Mirabel's and Emeka's POVs. At the reopened inquest into Ada's death, Emeka speaks in full sentences for the first time in twenty years, with Mirabel beside him. Daniel resigns from the bench rather than face cross-examination. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into voice.

chapters.title: Byline
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She publishes the whole story—her sister, her father, her cousin—in a long-form piece under her own name. Editors recoil, colleagues go quiet, and the smile that ends conversations finally fails her completely. Emotional beat: professional annihilation experienced as liberation.

chapters.title: What the Mouth Remembers
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Weeks later, eating alone in a cheap diner, she tastes her food—suddenly, overwhelmingly—for the first time since Ada died. She weeps into her plate among strangers. Emotional beat: the body forgiving what the mind confessed.

chapters.title: Ferrier Street, First Stop
chapters.summary: Mirabel's and Chidi's POVs. The siblings visit the fenced quarry one last time before demolition, leaving Ada's favorite sweets at the fence line. Chidi takes her hand—first physical contact between them in the novel. Emotional beat: mourning finally shared instead of managed.

chapters.title: The New Menu
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, epilogue. A year on: her career is smaller, her family imperfectly reconciled, Grace and Emeka part of her Sundays. Cooking for them, she burns the rice and laughs. The last bus to Ferrier Street is gone, but the street remains—in testimony, in print, in taste. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace without absolution.
